newsitem.title: THAILAND: Pol Pot's crimes didn't include genocide - article.
newsitem.headline: Pol Pot's crimes didn't include genocide - article.

text.p: A carefully staged trial of reviled Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot found the much-feared Cambodian guerrilla leader guilty of several crimes but not of genocide, an article on the trial showed on Thursday.

Pol Pot, the architect of the Khmer Rouge's 1975-79 "killing fields" rule during which more than a million Cambodians were killed by execution, torture, disease, starvation or hard labour, was sentenced to life imprisonment by his former comrades last week.
But his crimes did not include genocide, according to the article in the Far Eastern Economic Review which appeared on Thursday.
It was written by Nate Thayer, who, along with a cameraman, filmed and witnessed the trial and were the first journalists to see Pol Pot in 18 years.

"Pol Pot...is genuinely finished," Thayer wrote. "He has been denounced and imprisoned by his own movement. Not for the...Cambodian genocide, but for turning on his own comrades in an attempted purge in June, according to speakers at his trial."

Thayer said the ailing, white-haired Pol Pot sat with three other accused Khmer Rouge leaders in an open-air meeting hall in the jungle of northern Cambodia as speaker after speaker denounced them for their crimes and betrayal of the group during a brutal split of the rebel group in June.
The audience of about 500 people included many without limbs or missing eyes, others with wooden stumps, some sitting in wheelchairs -- all victims of Pol Pot's regime.

The secretive Maoist group split in early June after Pol Pot ordered a purge of top leaders who were involved in negotiations with officials from now-ousted premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party, the article said.

Ranariddh was ousted in a bloody July 5-6 power grab in Phnom Penh by his former co-premier Hun Sen. Hun Sen said at the time the fighting began because he was trying to stop Ranariddh from allowing Khmer Rouge to infiltrate the capital.

Thayer's article said Pol Pot launched a desperate attempt on June 9 to scuttle a peace deal with Ranariddh by purging top leader Ta Mok and others. That night he ordered the killing of long-time defence minister Son Sen and 14 of his relatives.
"'Having acknowledged the betrayal of our group in recent months by Pol Pot and his clique,' the loudspeaker roared into the nearby forest, then Pol Pot's 'crimes' were read out," the article said.

"They included the murder of Son Sen, the attempted murder and 'detention' of Ta Mok and Nuon Chea, and 'destroying the policy of national reconciliation', a reference to the attempt to block the FUNCINPEC deal," Thayer wrote.

"'These are the criminal acts -- the betrayal by Pol Pot and his clique -- against the people, armed forces and our cadre,'" the article quoted Mak Ben, a French-educated economist dressed in a green Chinese-style military uniform, as saying.
The tribunal sentenced Pol Pot to life imprisonment, but ruled out turning him over to international courts, it said.

Pol Pot knew his trial would be witnessed by Westerners, the article said, quoting a Khmer Rouge official who said the former leader had "consented" to a journalist's presence as a way of acknowledging his guilt.
One of the reasons the Khmer Rouge wanted to distance themselves from Pol Pot was to attract international support for their efforts to unseat Hun Sen, Thayer said.
Although speaker after speaker denounced Pol Pot, he was still treated with some respect, the article said.
"Some people respectfully bowed, as if to royalty, as Pol Pot walked 25 metres towards a waiting vehicle."
